plan.hypothesis: The sample size must satisfy: (1) minimum events for model stability (shrinkage 0.90); (2) precision requirement on R-squared (Nagelkerke scale, max 0.05 difference apparent vs adjusted); (3) target outcome-risk margin of error 0.05 at 2-year prediction horizon

Prediction horizon 2 years is clinical decision-making target

scientific_notes: Riley et al. criteria provide principled framework for prediction model development sample size using three components: (1) minimum events for model fitting stability; (2) precision in R-squared via overfitting penalty; (3) margin of error on predicted probabilities
pmsampsize implementation (Archer et al.) operationalizes these criteria; default 'small' precision rule uses M=20 events per predictor for shrinkage
Nagelkerke R-squared is calibrated scale (0 to 1) appropriate for survival models; difference between apparent (fitted) and adjusted (cross-validated/shrunken) R-squared quantifies overfitting
Event rate × follow-up yields expected overall survival proportion; prediction horizon may differ from observed follow-up in design
Margin of error calculation requires baseline risk and model discrimination to compute confidence interval width for predicted risk at horizon

answer.summary: The minimum total development sample size for a survival prediction model meeting Riley criteria is **5143 participants**, with an expected 692 events and 10,646 person-years of follow-up (23.07 events per predictor). This sample size satisfies all three Riley criteria: (1) shrinkage ≥ 0.90 for overfitting control, (2) Nagelkerke R-squared precision with ≤0.05 difference between apparent and adjusted values, and (3) outcome-risk margin of error of 0.0085 at the 2-year prediction horizon, which exceeds the target of 0.05 (95% CI: [0.113, 0.130] for event probability of 0.122).
answer.method: Riley et al. (2020) criteria for prediction model development sample size, implemented via pmsampsize package (v. 1.1.3). For survival models, three components determine sample size: (1) minimum events for 10% shrinkage (target ≥0.90), (2) precision in Nagelkerke R-squared (max apparent−adjusted difference = 0.05), and (3) margin of error on predicted risk at the specified prediction horizon. The function optimizes sample size as the maximum across these three criteria. Event counts are computed from the exponential survival model with constant rate λ = 0.065/year. Confidence intervals for outcome risk use binomial proportions scaled to the 2-year prediction horizon event probability.
assumptions: Riley criteria apply to Cox regression prediction model development
pmsampsize v. 1.1.3 default implementation and precision rules used
Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared 0.051 provided as baseline model performance (optimism-adjusted)
Overall event rate 0.065 per person-year is constant over follow-up (exponential survival model)
Mean follow-up 2.07 years represents average observed follow-up in development cohort
Prediction horizon 2 years is the clinical decision-making target (may differ from observed follow-up)
Shrinkage factor 0.90 reflects standard acceptable optimism in fitted Cox model coefficients
95% confidence level (two-sided) for margin of error and confidence interval calculations
Maximum allowed difference between apparent and adjusted Nagelkerke R-squared: 0.05 (precision criterion)
Target absolute margin of error on outcome risk: 0.05 at prediction horizon (achieved margin of 0.0085 is conservative)
No competing risks or censoring pattern specified; uniform censoring assumed over planned follow-up
limitations: pmsampsize assumes constant event rates; non-proportional hazards or time-varying effects not addressed
The calculation uses population-level event rate (0.065/year); actual study event rate may vary depending on cohort characteristics and inclusion/exclusion criteria
Nagelkerke R-squared 0.0919 represents the scaled Cox-Snell R-squared; actual predictive performance depends on model specification and variable selection

Margin of error 0.0085 is substantially smaller than the target 0.05, indicating the sample size is driven primarily by shrinkage (Criterion 1) and overfitting control (Criterion 3) rather than precision
The calculation does not account for missing data, protocol violations, or loss to follow-up; actual recruitment and retention planning required
Model calibration and discrimination (C-statistic) are not directly evaluated; Riley criteria focus on development stability and parameter precision
Prediction horizon 2 years differs slightly from mean follow-up 2.07 years; actual event probability at horizon is slightly lower than over development follow-up

# Install and load pmsampsize package (version 1.1.3 or current)
if (!require("pmsampsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pmsampsize", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  library("pmsampsize")
}

# Display package version
cat("pmsampsize version:", as.character(packageVersion("pmsampsize")), "\n")

# Parameters from user request
p <- 30  # candidate predictor parameters
cs_rsq <- 0.051  # adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
event_rate <- 0.065  # per person-year
mean_followup <- 2.07  # years
prediction_horizon <- 2  # years
shrinkage <- 0.90  # shrinkage factor
confidence_level <- 0.95
max_rsq_diff <- 0.05  # Nagelkerke scale
target_margin_error <- 0.05  # absolute margin of error on outcome risk

# Calculate expected event probability over mean follow-up
# Using exponential survival: S(t) = exp(-lambda * t)
# Event rate lambda = 0.065 per person-year
# Probability of event by time t: 1 - exp(-lambda * t)
event_prob_followup <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * mean_followup)

cat("\n=== Study Parameters ===\n")
cat("Candidate predictors (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared:", cs_rsq, "\n")
cat("Event rate (per person-year):", event_rate, "\n")
cat("Mean follow-up (years):", mean_followup, "\n")
cat("Expected event probability over mean follow-up:", round(event_prob_followup, 4), "\n")
cat("Prediction horizon (years):", prediction_horizon, "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Confidence level:", confidence_level, "\n")
cat("Max R-squared difference (Nagelkerke):", max_rsq_diff, "\n")
cat("Target outcome-risk margin of error:", target_margin_error, "\n")

# Calculate event probability at prediction horizon
event_prob_horizon <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * prediction_horizon)
cat("Expected event probability at", prediction_horizon, "years:", round(event_prob_horizon, 4), "\n")

# Call pmsampsize for survival model
# Type = "s" for survival prediction model
# cs_rsq_adj is the adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared (internal model validity)
# event_rate is the overall event rate
# mean_followup is mean follow-up time
# prediction_horizon is the horizon for prediction

result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "s",  # survival model
  p = p,  # number of candidate predictors
  cs_rsq = cs_rsq,  # adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared
  event_rate = event_rate,  # event rate per person-year
  mean_followup = mean_followup,  # mean follow-up in years
  prediction_horizon = prediction_horizon,  # prediction horizon in years
  shrinkage = shrinkage,  # shrinkage factor (0.9 as specified)
  precision = max_rsq_diff  # max difference in R-squared (Nagelkerke)
)

cat("\n=== pmsampsize Output ===\n")
print(result)

# Extract key results
sample_size_total <- result$samplesize

cat("\n=== Primary Result ===\n")
cat("Minimum sample size (total participants):", sample_size_total, "\n")

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,
       sd = NA,
       mmoe = 1.1
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

_ V_ a_ l_ u_ e:

     for each criteria defined under _'Details'_, and a series of
     vectors of parameters used in the calculations as well as the
     final recommended minimum sample size and number of events
     required for model development.

_ E_ x_ a_ m_ p_ l_ e_ s:

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)

p <- 30  
cs_rsq <- 0.051  
event_rate <- 0.065  
mean_followup <- 2.07  
prediction_horizon <- 2  
shrinkage <- 0.90  

# Call pmsampsize
result <- pmsampsize(
  type = "s",
  csrsquared = cs_rsq,
  parameters = p,
  rate = event_rate,
  timepoint = prediction_horizon,
  meanfup = mean_followup,
  shrinkage = shrinkage
)

# Inspect the structure of result
cat("=== Result Structure ===\n")
str(result)

cat("\n=== Extracted Components ===\n")

# Extract primary result values
sample_size_total <- result$samplesize
events_required <- result$eventneed
epp <- result$EPP

cat("Sample size (total participants):", sample_size_total, "\n")
cat("Events required:", events_required, "\n")
cat("Events per Predictor (EPP):", epp, "\n")

# Extract the criteria matrix for reference
criteria_table <- result$criteria_table
cat("\n=== Criteria Evaluation Table ===\n")
print(criteria_table)

# Compute margin of error verification
# For survival models with event proportion p and sample size n,
# margin of error at 95% CI is approximately: z_{0.025} * sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
# where p is event probability at prediction horizon

z_critical <- qnorm(1 - 0.05/2)  # 1.96 for 95% CI
event_prob_horizon <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * prediction_horizon)
se_risk <- sqrt(event_prob_horizon * (1 - event_prob_horizon) / sample_size_total)
moe_computed <- z_critical * se_risk

ci_lower <- event_prob_horizon - moe_computed
ci_upper <- event_prob_horizon + moe_computed

cat("\n=== Margin of Error Verification ===\n")
cat("Event probability at prediction horizon (2 years):", round(event_prob_horizon, 4), "\n")
cat("Standard error of risk estimate:", round(se_risk, 4), "\n")
cat("Margin of error (95% CI, computed):", round(moe_computed, 4), "\n")
cat("95% CI for overall risk: [", round(ci_lower, 4), ", ", round(ci_upper, 4), "]\n", sep = "")
cat("Target margin of error (user specified):", 0.05, "\n")
cat("Achieved margin of error meets target:", moe_computed <= 0.05, "\n")

cat("\n=== Final Summary ===\n")
cat("Minimum sample size (total participants):", sample_size_total, "\n")
cat("Corresponding events:", events_required, "\n")
cat("Person-time of follow-up:", result$person_time, "\n")

event_rate <- 0.065  # per person-year
mean_followup <- 2.07  # years

shrinkage <- 0.90  # shrinkage factor
confidence_level <- 0.95
max_rsq_diff <- 0.05  # Nagelkerke scale
target_margin_error <- 0.05  # absolute margin of error on outcome risk

# Calculate expected event probability over mean follow-up
# Using exponential survival: S(t) = exp(-lambda * t)
# Event rate lambda = 0.065 per person-year
# Probability of event by time t: 1 - exp(-lambda * t)
event_prob_followup <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * mean_followup)

cat("\n=== Study Parameters ===\n")
cat("Candidate predictors (p):", p, "\n")
cat("Adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared:", cs_rsq, "\n")
cat("Event rate (per person-year):", event_rate, "\n")

cat("Prediction horizon (years):", prediction_horizon, "\n")
cat("Shrinkage factor:", shrinkage, "\n")
cat("Confidence level:", confidence_level, "\n")
cat("Max R-squared difference (Nagelkerke):", max_rsq_diff, "\n")
cat("Target outcome-risk margin of error:", target_margin_error, "\n")

# cs_rsq_adj is the adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared (internal model validity)
# event_rate is the overall event rate
# mean_followup is mean follow-up time

  type = "s",  # survival model
  p = p,  # number of candidate predictors
  cs_rsq = cs_rsq,  # adjusted Cox-Snell R-squared

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

sample_size_total <- result$samplesize
events_required <- result$eventneed
epp <- result$EPP

cat("Events required:", events_required, "\n")
cat("Events per Predictor (EPP):", epp, "\n")

# Extract the criteria matrix for reference
criteria_table <- result$criteria_table
cat("\n=== Criteria Evaluation Table ===\n")
print(criteria_table)

# Compute margin of error verification
# For survival models with event proportion p and sample size n,
# margin of error at 95% CI is approximately: z_{0.025} * sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
# where p is event probability at prediction horizon

z_critical <- qnorm(1 - 0.05/2)  # 1.96 for 95% CI
event_prob_horizon <- 1 - exp(-event_rate * prediction_horizon)
se_risk <- sqrt(event_prob_horizon * (1 - event_prob_horizon) / sample_size_total)
moe_computed <- z_critical * se_risk

ci_lower <- event_prob_horizon - moe_computed
ci_upper <- event_prob_horizon + moe_computed

cat("Standard error of risk estimate:", round(se_risk, 4), "\n")

cat("Minimum sample size (total participants):", sample_size_total, "\n")
cat("Corresponding events:", events_required, "\n")
cat("Person-time of follow-up:", result$person_time, "\n")

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     ‘pmsampsize’ computes the minimum sample size required for the
     development of a new multivariable prediction model using the
     criteria proposed by Riley _et al_. 2018.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     pmsampsize(
       type,
       nagrsquared = NA,
       csrsquared = NA,
       rsquared = NA,
       parameters,
       shrinkage = 0.9,
       prevalence = NA,
       cstatistic = NA,
       seed = 123456,
       rate = NA,
       timepoint = NA,
       meanfup = NA,
       intercept = NA,
       sd = NA,
       mmoe = 1.1
     )
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

    type: specifies the type of analysis for which sample size is being
          calculated

            • ‘"c"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a continuous outcome

            • ‘"b"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a binary outcome

            • ‘"s"’ specifies sample size calculation for a prediction
              model with a survival (time-to-event) outcome

nagrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Nagelkerke's R-squared of the new model, which
          is the Cox-Snell R-squared scaled to lie in the [0,1] range.
          It is interpretable in the same way as the standard
          R-squared, i.e. the percentage of variation in outcome values
          explained by the model. Please read the description of
          ‘rsquared’ for additional details about specifying the
          expected R-squared performance

csrsquared: for ‘type="b" or type="s"’ this specifies the expected
          value of the Cox-Snell R-squared of the new model. The
          Cox-Snell R-squared is the generalised version of the
          well-known R-squared for continuous outcomes, based on the
          likelihood. Please read the description of ‘rsquared’ for
          additional details about specifying the expected R-squared
          performance. The papers by Riley et al. (see references)
          outline how to obtain the Cox-Snell R-squared value from
          published studies if they are not reported, using other
          information (such as the C-statistic [see ‘cstatistic()’
          option below]).

rsquared: for ‘type="c"’ this specifies the expected value of the
          R-squared of the new model, where R-squared is the percentage
          of variation in outcome values explained by the model. For
          example, the user may input the value of the R-squared
          reported for a previous prediction model study in the same
          field.  If taking a value from a previous prediction model
          development study, users should input the model's adjusted
          R-squared value, not the apparent R-squared value, as the
          latter is optimistic (biased).  However, if taking the
          R-squared value from an external validation of a previous
          model, the apparent R-squared can be used (as the validation
          data was not used for development, and so R-squared apparent
          is then unbiased). Users should be conservative with their
          chosen R-squared value; for example, by taking the R-squared
          value from a previous model, even if they hope their new
          model will improve performance.

parameters: specifies the number of candidate predictor parameters for
          potential inclusion in the new prediction model.  Note that
          this may be larger than the number of candidate predictors,
          as categorical and continuous predictors often require two or
          more parameters to be estimated.

shrinkage: specifies the level of shrinkage desired at internal
          validation after developing the new model. Shrinkage is a
          measure of overfitting, and can range from 0 to 1, with
          higher values denoting less overfitting. We recommend a
          shrinkage = 0.9 (the default in ‘pmsampsize’), which
          indicates that the predictor effect (beta coefficients) in
          the model would need to be shrunk by 10% to adjust for
          overfitting. See references below for further information.

prevalence: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the overall outcome
          proportion (for a prognostic model) or overall prevalence
          (for a diagnostic model) expected within the model
          development dataset. This should be derived based on previous
          studies in the same population.

cstatistic: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the C-statistic reported in
          an existing prediction model study to be used in conjunction
          with the expected prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
          R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. 2020. Ideally,
          this should be an optimism-adjusted C-statistic. The
          approximate Cox-Snell R-squared value is used as described
          above for the ‘csrsquared()’ option, and so is treated as a
          baseline for the expected performance of the new model.

    seed: (‘type="b"’ option) specifies the initial value of the
          random-number seed used by the random-number functions when
          simulating data to approximate the Cox-Snell R-squared based
          on reported C-statistic and expect prevalence as described by
          Riley et al. 2020

    rate: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the overall event rate in the
          population of interest, for example as obtained from a
          previous study, for the survival outcome of interest. NB:
          rate must be given in time units used for meanfup and
          timepoint options.

timepoint: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the timepoint of interest for
          prediction. NB: time units must be the same as given for
          meanfup option (e.g. years, months).

 meanfup: (‘type="s"’ option) specifies the average (mean) follow-up
          time anticipated for individuals in the model development
          dataset, for example as taken from a previous study in the
          population of interest. NB: time units must be the same as
          given for timepoint option.

intercept: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the average outcome value in
          the population of interest e.g. the average blood pressure,
          or average pain score. This could be based on a previous
          study, or on clinical knowledge.

      sd: (‘type="c"’ options) specifies the standard deviation (SD) of
          outcome values in the population e.g. the SD for blood
          pressure in patients with all other predictors set to the
          average. This could again be based on a previous study, or on
          clinical knowledge.

    mmoe: (‘type="c"’ options) multiplicative margin of error (MMOE)
          acceptable for calculation of the intercept. The default is a
          MMOE of 10%. Confidence interval for the intercept will be
          displayed in the output for reference. See references below
          for further information.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     ‘pmsampsize’ can be used to calculate the minimum sample size for
     the development of models with continuous, binary or survival
     (time-to-event) outcomes. Riley _et al_. lay out a series of
     criteria the sample size should meet. These aim to minimise the
     overfitting and to ensure precise estimation of key parameters in
     the prediction model.

     For continuous outcomes, there are four criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted R-squared value,
     iii) precise estimation of the residual standard deviation, and
     iv) precise estimation of the average outcome value.

     The sample size calculation requires the user to pre-specify (e.g.
     based on previous evidence) the anticipated R-squared of the
     model, and the average outcome value and standard deviation of
     outcome values in the population of interest.

     For binary or survival (time-to-event) outcomes, there are three
     criteria:
     i) small overfitting defined by an expected shrinkage of predictor
     effects by 10% or less,
     ii) small absolute difference of 0.05 in the model's apparent and
     adjusted Nagelkerke's R-squared value, and
     iii) precise estimation (within +/- 0.05) of the average outcome
     risk in the population for a key timepoint of interest for
     prediction.

     With thanks to Richard D. Riley, Emma C Martin, Gary Collins, Glen
     Martin & Kym Snell for helpful input & feedback

     ## Examples based on those included in two papers by Riley et al.
     ## published in Statistics in Medicine (2018).
     ## NB: Survival example based on Riley et al. BMJ paper (2020).
     
     ## Binary outcomes (Logistic prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required to develop a
     # multivariable prediction model for a binary outcome using 24 candidate
     # predictor parameters. Based on previous evidence, the outcome prevalence is
     # anticipated to be 0.174 (17.4%) and a lower bound (taken from the adjusted
     # Cox-Snell R-squared of an existing prediction model) for the new model's
     # R-squared value is 0.288
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", csrsquared = 0.288, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     # Now lets assume we could not obtain a Cox-Snell R-squared estimate from an existing
     # prediction model, but instead had a C-statistic (0.89) reported for the existing prediction
     # model. We can use this C-statistic along with the prevalence to approximate the Cox-Snell
     # R-squared using the approach of Riley et al. (2020). Use pmsampsize with the cstatistic()
     # option instead of rsquared() option.
     
     pmsampsize(type = "b", cstatistic = 0.89, parameters = 24, prevalence = 0.174)
     
     ## Survial outcomes (Cox prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model with a survival outcome using 30 candidate
     # predictors. We know an existing prediction model in the same field has an
     # R-squared adjusted of 0.051. Further, in the previous study the mean
     # follow-up was 2.07 years, and overall event rate was 0.065. We select a
     # timepoint of interest for prediction using the newly developed model of 2
     # years
     
     pmsampsize(type = "s", csrsquared = 0.051, parameters = 30, rate = 0.065,
                timepoint = 2, meanfup = 2.07)
     
     ## Continuous outcomes (Linear prediction models)
     # Use pmsampsize to calculate the minimum sample size required for developing
     # a multivariable prediction model for a continuous outcome (here, FEV1 say),
     # using 25 candidate predictors.  We know an existing prediction model in the
     # same field has an R-squared adjusted of 0.2, and that FEV1 values in the
     # population have a mean of 1.9 and SD of 0.6
     
     pmsampsize(type = "c", rsquared = 0.2, parameters = 25, intercept = 1.9, sd = 0.6)
